entry.title: 3DCityDB (v 4.0.0) Setup Guide for Absolute Beginners (Part 2)
entry.content:
Everything you need to install before building your first 3D city digital twin

Part 1

Digital Twin Foundations (Part 1): Where Cities Learn, Think, & Evolve

If you read the previous blog, you now understand what digital twins are and why they matter for modern cities. Now we move one step forward — from theory to hands-on practice.

Before we install and use 3DCityDB, one of the world’s most widely adopted open-source platforms for managing 3D city models, it’s important to understand the software components you’ll need.

This guide breaks down each requirement in simple terms:

  • What it is
  • Why do you need it for 3DCityDB
  • Where do you download it

By the end, you’ll have a complete checklist ready for installing your first 3DCityDB environment.

A database is basically a smart, organized digital cupboard where you store information so that you can easily search it, update it, sort it, or analyze it whenever you need.

Think of it like this:

  • A notebook can store information, but finding a specific detail later is hard.
  • A spreadsheet helps a bit, but once the data becomes huge, it becomes slow and messy.
  • A database, on the other hand, is designed to handle huge volumes of information — millions of records — smoothly and efficiently.

It’s like having a librarian who instantly knows:

  • where every book is,
  • what’s inside it,
  • how it connects to other books,
  • and can answer complex questions in seconds.

Imagine you have a city with:

  • 50,000 buildings
  • Every building has floors, walls, roofs, materials, textures, and geometry
  • and each of those having coordinates, heights, attributes, and relationships

Putting all of this in one file (like a spreadsheet or XML file) would quickly become unmanageable.
It would be:

  • slow to open
  • impossible to query
  • hard to search
  • difficult to maintain

But in a database?

You can instantly ask questions like:

  • “Show me all buildings taller than 30 meters.”
  • “Find all buildings within 500 meters of a school.”
  • “Give me only the LoD2 buildings with roof textures.”

And you get answers in seconds, not hours.

📌 Another Simple Analogy: Your Phone Contacts

Your phone’s Contacts app is a tiny database.
It stores:

  • names
  • phone numbers
  • emails
  • photos

If you search “Amit,” it instantly finds Amit — even if you have 2,000 contacts.
That’s the power of a database: fast, organized retrieval.

Now imagine the same idea, but instead of 2,000 contacts, you have 2 million building components.
That’s exactly why city-scale digital twins use databases.

3D city models like CityGML are extremely detailed. A single building might include:

  • 3D coordinates
  • roof and wall surfaces
  • windows and doors
  • textures
  • attributes (height, function, construction year)
  • relationships (building part, parent building)
  • multiple levels of detail (LoD1 to LoD4)

If you store this in a simple file, it becomes huge and slow.

A spatial database like PostgreSQL + PostGIS:

  • stores everything in clean tables
  • keeps geometry indexed
  • allows fast 3D queries
  • supports city-scale datasets (entire Berlin, Singapore, Rotterdam, etc.)

This is why 3DCityDB exists — it gives cities a powerful way to store, manage, analyze, and export complex 3D city models efficiently.

🌆 What Is 3DCityDB?

3DCityDB is one of the most important open-source technologies in the world of 3D city modelling and digital twins. At its core, it is a database schema and toolkit designed specifically for storing, managing, querying, and exporting CityGML-based 3D city models. While many tools can view or draw 3D buildings, very few can store and manage large-scale semantic city models efficiently — and that is exactly where 3DCityDB stands out.

Developed originally by the Chair of Geoinformatics at the Technical University of Munich (TUM), along with virtualcitySYSTEMS and M.O.S.S., 3DCityDB has grown into a global standard. Cities like Berlin, New York, Rotterdam, Zurich, and Singapore have used it to manage their 3D city models internally or to power public digital twin portals.

What makes 3DCityDB special is that it treats a city not merely as geometry but as a semantic structure: buildings with roofs, walls, functions, heights, LODs, attributes, and relationships. All of this detail is stored inside a relational database (PostgreSQL/PostGIS or Oracle), which allows the city model to behave like a living dataset rather than a static 3D file.

Think of it as the central brain of your 3D city digital twin. It allows you to:

  • Store city models in a relational (table-based) database
  • Query and analyze 3D objects
  • Export to CityGML, KML, COLLADA, glTF, and 3D Tiles
  • Visualize city models via its Web Map Client (Cesium-based)
  • Link external data like spreadsheets or IoT attributes

This makes 3DCityDB a foundational tool for digital twins, urban planning, city-scale simulations, and web-based 3D visualization.

Why Was 3DCityDB Created?

Traditional 3D formats (OBJ, glTF, shapefiles) are excellent for visualization but fall short when you need to:

  • store millions of real buildings
  • handle multiple Levels of Detail (LoD0–LoD4)
  • preserve semantic and thematic information
  • run spatial queries
  • manage textures, roofs, façades, terrain, vegetation
  • export into standards like CityGML, KML, COLLADA, or 3D Tiles

A typical CityGML dataset may contain hundreds of thousands of objects, each with detailed geometries, attributes, hierarchies, and metadata. Storing this in files becomes slow, messy, and impossible to query efficiently.

3DCityDB solves this by providing:

  • a relational database schema for every CityGML feature
  • prebuilt spatial indexes for fast queries
  • tools to import and export CityGML at scale
  • web-based visualization using Cesium
  • scripts for managing textures and 3D objects
  • compatibility with modeling, GIS, and digital twin workflows

It is essentially the backbone of many large digital twin initiatives around the world.

Here’s what you can achieve once 3DCityDB is set up:

Store a full 3D city model — Buildings, terrain, surfaces, appearance data, bridges, tunnels, vegetation — everything goes into structured database tables instead of giant XML files.

Query the city like a dataset — You can run SQL queries such as:

  • Find all buildings higher than 40 meters
  • Export only LoD2 models with textures
  • Select all buildings within 300 meters of a given road

This makes it powerful for planners, researchers, and digital twin developers.

Import and export complex datasets — Using the Importer/Exporter tool, you can move data between: CityGML, KML, COLLADA, glTF, 3D Tiles (for Cesium), and Spread­sheets (with plugins). This makes 3DCityDB extremely versatile — you can prepare datasets for web visualization, simulations, BIM workflows, and more.

Visualize the city on the web — The Web Map Client lets you load your exported 3D model into a Cesium-based viewer directly in a browser, enabling: interactive navigation, attribute exploration, public dashboards, and digital twin prototypes. It runs locally or on any server with minimal setup.

Why Is 3DCityDB Important Today?

In the age of smart cities and digital twins, cities generate enormous amounts of spatial data. 3DCityDB offers a stable, well-documented, and free foundation for:

  • urban simulations
  • energy modeling
  • disaster risk assessments
  • planning and zoning
  • infrastructure management
  • 3D web visualization
  • AI/ML-based city analytics

Its combination of semantic detail, scalable storage, and open standards makes it one of the most future-proof solutions available.

Preparing the Course Data

Before we begin working with 3DCityDB, we’ll need a sample dataset to practice with. For this and further tutorials, we’ll use a training package provided by the 3DCityDB team. It contains everything we need: a CityGML file from Berlin, folders for storing exports, and a simple local web server for visualizing results later in the course. You can download the dataset from the link below:

👉 Download tutorial data:
https://www.3dcitydb.de/3dcitydb/fileadmin/TUM_Workshop/RTG_Schulungskurs_2016.zip

Once the ZIP file finishes downloading, extract the contents into the following directory :

C:\RTG_Schulungskurs_2016

After unzipping, your folder structure should look similar to the one shown in the tutorial screenshot. Here’s what each part of the directory is for:

When extracted correctly on Windows, the folder will contain several key components that we’ll use during the tutorial:

  • CityGML-Data — This is the main dataset we’ll work with. It contains a CityGML file representing 950+ textured buildings from a district in Berlin. Throughout the exercises, we’ll import this file into the database, analyze it, export it in different formats, and eventually visualize it on the web.
  • Exports — This folder is where all the outputs you generate during the exercises will be saved. Inside, you’ll find three pre-made subdirectories — one each for CityGML, KML, and spreadsheet exports.
  • node_modules and server.js — These files together form a lightweight Node.js web server. We’ll use it later in the course to host the 3DCityDB Web Map client locally and preview the 3D city model in a browser.

By setting up these folders beforehand, your entire workflow — from importing data into 3DCityDB to exporting visualizations and generating spreadsheets — will stay organized and easy to navigate.

Software Installations

3DCityDB is not a standalone app — it relies on a set of supporting software components.

  1. Java (JRE 8 or higher)
  2. PostgreSQL + PostGIS
  3. 3DCityDB SQL Scripts
  4. 3DCityDB Importer-Exporter Tool
  5. Spreadsheet-Generator-Plugin
  6. 3DCityDB-Web-Map
  7. Node.js
  8. Google Earth Pro

Now that you have a quick overview of the tools involved, let’s begin with the first building block: Java.

1. Java (JRE 8 or higher)

What is Java?

Java is a widely used programming language that enables applications to run on various operating systems. Many geospatial tools—including the 3DCityDB Importer/Exporter—are built using Java because of its stability, portability, and powerful runtime environment.

Why does 3DCityDB need Java?
The Importer/Exporter tool of 3DCityDB is a Java-based application. That means it cannot run unless your system has a Java Runtime Environment (JRE) installed. Without Java, the Importer/Exporter tool simply won’t open.

In short:

✔ 3DCityDB relies on Java
✔ Java provides the runtime needed to execute the tool
✔ Every OS (Windows, macOS, Linux) must install Java before proceeding

📥 Download Link

Download Java

How to Install Java (Step-by-Step)

Follow these steps to install the correct Java version for your system.

  1. Open the official Java download page:
    https://java.com/en/download/manual.jsp
    (This is the trusted source for Java downloads.)
  2. Choose the version for your operating system
    You’ll see options for Windows, macOS, Linux, and Solaris.
  3. Download the installer
    For Windows, this will be an .exe file.
    For macOS, it will be a .dmg file.
  4. Run the installer
    Double-click the downloaded file.
  5. Follow the on-screen instructions
    Installation is simple — just click Next → Next → Finish.
  6. Verify installation (optional but recommended)
    On Windows:
    Open Command Prompt → type:
java -version

If installed correctly, you’ll see something like:java version "1.8.x"

With Java in place, the next crucial component is the spatial database that powers the entire 3DCityDB environment.

2. PostgreSQL + PostGIS

Before we install anything else, it’s important to understand that 3DCityDB runs entirely on a spatial database. This database is where every building, geometry, texture, and semantic attribute will live. Without a proper database engine, 3DCityDB simply cannot function.

PostgreSQL — The main database

PostgreSQL is a popular open-source relational database. Think of it as the “brain” that stores all the CityGML objects — buildings, surfaces, roofs, terrain, windows, and even metadata.

PostGIS — The spatial extension

PostGIS adds support for geometry, 3D coordinates, spatial indexing, and spatial queries. 3DCityDB relies heavily on these features, especially when working with CityGML files containing thousands (or millions) of geometries.

Why do we need a database in the first place?

3D city models are far more complex than simple 2D GIS shapefiles. A typical CityGML file may contain:

  • Multi-LOD building geometries
  • Surface boundaries and edges
  • Roof and wall surfaces
  • Textures and materials
  • Semantic attributes
  • Terrain objects
  • City furniture
  • Vegetation
  • Bridges, tunnels, transportation networks
  • Metadata and relationships between components

Storing all this inside an XML or GIS file quickly becomes inefficient. A spatial database solves several issues:

✔ Efficient storage for large models — CityGML datasets of real cities easily reach several gigabytes. A database handles this scale smoothly.

✔ Spatial indexing-To retrieve a single building or a specific coordinate location, the database uses R-Tree spatial indexes — much faster than reading entire files.

✔ Fast querying-You can run SQL queries like:

  • “Select all buildings higher than 30 meters.”
  • “Find buildings within 500 meters of a metro station.”
  • “Export only LoD2 models of district A.”

✔ Semantic relationships-Buildings aren’t just shapes — they have attributes. PostgreSQL + PostGIS stores all those relationships cleanly and efficiently.

✔ Free and widely supported — Although 3DCityDB also supports Oracle, PostgreSQL is the easiest and most widely used option in the community.

Where to Download

You can download all required components from the official sources:

📥 Download PostgreSQL/PostGIS:

Downloads

📥 Download pgAdmin (optional, GUI tool):

Download

Installing PostgreSQL on Windows (Step-by-Step)

Go to the PostgreSQL download page.

Select your operating system and click 'Download the installer'.

Download the file (e.g., postgresql-18.1–1-windows-x64.exe).

Double-click the installer to install PostgreSQL in your system.

Click Yes on the User Account Control window. Continue through the setup with default options.

After installation, click Finish. The StackBuilder window will open.

Click Next to install additional components.

Expand Spatial Extensions and check PostGIS 3.6 Bundle for PostgreSQL 18.

Complete the installation with default options.

Download PgAdmin4

Visit the pgAdmin download page. Select Windows.

Download and install normally — no special configuration needed.

This will download the .exe installer. Double-click and install it.

PostgreSQL + PostGIS is the foundation of everything you will build in this tutorial series. Once your spatial database is ready, you can begin creating your 3DCityDB instance, importing CityGML datasets, and exploring your first digital twin.

Before the database can understand CityGML, we need to prepare it with the right structure, which is where the 3DCityDB SQL scripts come in.

3. 3DCityDB SQL Scripts

These scripts create the entire CityGML schema inside PostgreSQL.

Why is it needed?
PostgreSQL cannot understand CityGML by itself. The scripts:

  • create 70+ relational tables
  • define geometry relationships
  • set up indexes
  • build the internal structure of the city model

Note: If you install the Importer/Exporter (next step), the scripts come bundled automatically. No need for separate installation.

📥 Download scripts:

https://www.3dcitydb.org/3dcitydb/downloads/

  • 3D City Database
  • Releases · 3dcitydb/3dcitydb

The next step is to bring data in and out of the system — this is where the Importer/Exporter becomes your main interface.

4. 3DCityDB Importer/Exporter Tool

The Importer/Exporter tool is the workhorse of the entire 3DCityDB environment. Once your database is ready, this is the application that actually moves data in and out of the system. Whether you want to load a CityGML dataset into PostgreSQL or export your 3D city model into formats like KML, COLLADA, or glTF for visualization, this tool handles it all.

Unlike many GIS/BIM tools that hide their internal processes, the Importer/Exporter gives you full control over how CityGML objects are validated, stored, textured, and exported. If you plan to do anything serious with CityGML, this tool becomes essential very quickly.

Usage:

You will use the Importer/Exporter tool whenever you need to:

  • Import CityGML files (LoD0–LoD4) into PostgreSQL/PostGIS
  • Export 3D city data into KML/COLLADA/glTF for Google Earth, Cesium, or other 3D platforms
  • Validate datasets before they go into the database
  • Apply tiling strategies (useful for large cities)
  • Manage textures and surface geometries
  • Generate spreadsheets of building attributes (with the plugin)

In practice, the Importer/Exporter becomes the “control room” for interacting with your 3D city database. A few reasons this tool is at the center of any 3DCityDB workflow:

  • It handles large datasets efficiently — CityGML files, especially those of LoD2 or LoD3, can be enormous. The tool is optimized to process them.
  • It understands CityGML semantics — Instead of simply loading geometry, it preserves building attributes, names, functions, floors, roof types, and more.
  • Exports are plug-and-play for visualization — The glTF/KML/COLLADA exports work instantly with tools like Cesium Web Viewer, Google Earth Pro, and custom 3D engines.
  • No complicated setup required — The installer configures everything, so you can start importing CityGML files within minutes.
  • Open-source and actively supported — You always know what’s happening under the hood, which makes debugging and research much easier.

Download the Importer/Exporter Tool

Download link -

Release v4.1.0 · 3dcitydb/importer-exporter

Getting the tool is straightforward:

  1. Visit the official 3DCityDB importer-exporter GitHub repo page:
    https://github.com/3dcitydb/importer-exporter

2. Once you open the page, scroll down to the Releases section and look for Version 4.1.0. Under Assets, download the setup file named:

3DCityDB-Importer-Exporter-4.1.0-Setup.jar

This file contains the installer.

4. After the .jar file has finished downloading, simply double-click it to launch the installer. You’ll be greeted with the setup wizard. The first page of the installation wizard looks like the following figure.

Select your preferred language and click on OK. Run the installer and follow the on-screen steps. Click on the Next button to continue the installation process.

On the License Agreement page, you should read the license agreement.  Check the radio button — I accept the terms of the license agreement. Click on the Next button to continue the installation process

On the Select Destination Location page, browse to the folder where the tutorial dataset is stored, create a new folder named, and select that folder path as the installation path.

Click the Next button on the wizard.

The installer may ask whether it can create or overwrite a folder — select OK/YES to proceed.

For subsequent steps, keep the default settings and click on the Next button to continue the installation process.

Now, the selected installation packages are going to be installed on your machine.

You can now launch the tool directly using the desktop shortcut. A splash screen will appear for a moment before the main interface opens.

The Importer/Exporter window is your command center for interacting with CityGML datasets — importing files, validating them, exporting 3D formats, linking external attributes, and managing your database content. Let's proceed with the next tool…

5. Spreadsheet Generator Plugin (Optional)

The Importer/Exporter Tool becomes even more useful when you add plugins, and one of the most practical extensions is the Spreadsheet-Generator Plugin. As the name suggests, this plugin lets you turn the contents of your 3DCityDB database into easy-to-use tables — either CSV files or Excel spreadsheets. This is extremely handy when you want to inspect attributes, share datasets with colleagues, or run analysis in tools like Excel, Python, or Power BI.

The best part is that you don’t have to install it separately. While setting up the Importer/Exporter Tool, the installer would have prompted you with an option to include the Spreadsheet-Generator. Simply enable it, and the plugin becomes available inside the tool right away. If you’re curious about the inner workings or want to explore or modify the code, the plugin’s repository is publicly available on GitHub.

This plugin adds a very practical capability: it bridges the detailed 3D world of CityGML with the familiar tabular world of spreadsheets — making your 3DCityDB projects much easier to examine, report, and share.

📥 Plugin repo:

GitHub - 3dcitydb/plugin-spreadsheet-generator: Importer/Exporter plugin to export feature attributes as spreadsheets

Once your data is inside the database and ready for export, you’ll eventually want to see your city model, which brings us to the Web Map Client.

6. 3DCityDB Web Map Client

One of the most exciting parts of working with 3DCityDB is being able to see your 3D city model in action. The Web Map Client is the tool that makes this possible. It’s a lightweight, browser-based 3D viewer built on top of Cesium, and it allows you to explore your CityGML models interactively — no additional plugins or special software required.

What it is

The Web Map Client is essentially a ready-to-use WebGL application that can display 3D buildings, textures, attributes, and geometry stored in your 3DCityDB. It is written entirely in HTML and JavaScript, which means it runs in any modern browser and can be deployed on almost any web server with minimal setup.

Why it’s useful

Most of your work in 3DCityDB — importing CityGML, creating City Models, exporting data — happens behind the scenes. The Web Map Client brings that work to life. With it, you can:

  • Pan, zoom, and navigate around your 3D city
  • Click on buildings to inspect their attributes
  • Turn layers on and off
  • View different Levels of Detail
  • Present your models to stakeholders in an interactive format
  • Build early versions of a city-scale digital twin dashboard

For workshops, demonstrations, or digital-twin prototyping, this tool becomes indispensable.

Download

The Web Map Client is included in the Importer/Exporter installation, but you can also download it separately:

📥 GitHub Repository:

https://github.com/3dcitydb/3dcitydb-web-map

This repo contains: the full source code, documentation, configuration examples, and instructions for deployment.

Run it online instantly

If you want to try it without installing anything, the 3DCityDB team hosts a live version:

🌐 Online Viewer:

3DCityDB-Web-Map-Client

To run the Web Map Client locally, we need a lightweight server — this is where Node.js becomes essential.

7. Node.js (Required for This Tutorial)

When working with the 3DCityDB Web Map Client, one thing you quickly realize is that the viewer cannot be opened by simply double-clicking an HTML file. Modern browsers block certain features — such as loading local 3D Tiles, textures, or JSON files — unless they are served through a proper web server. This is where Node.js comes in.

Node.js is a lightweight JavaScript runtime that makes it extremely easy to spin up a small local server on your machine. The Cesium team, which developed the underlying viewer, designed a simple JavaScript-based server that runs on Node.js, allowing you to host the 3D Web Client with just a couple of commands.

In the context of this 3DCityDB tutorial, Node.js is essential because it lets you:

  • run the Cesium-based 3D viewer directly from your computer
  • load CityGML exports, 3D Tiles, glTF, and textures into the browser
  • test and interact with your city model before deploying it
  • mimic a real web server environment without complex configuration

Once Node.js is installed, starting the local server becomes incredibly straightforward — you simply run the provided server.js file from the dataset folder, and your browser will open to an interactive 3D view of Berlin's buildings.

📥 Download

Node.js - Run JavaScript Everywhere

Click on the Windows Installer (.msi) button and download the node-v24.11.1-x64.msi file. Double-click the installer to install it and continue with the instructions as prompted.

Keep the default options and proceed with the installation.

After clicking on Finish, the command prompt window opens automatically. Read the text and then press any key to continue.

Windows PowerShell opens automatically. Let it run its process completely. It will close by itself.

Finally, to double-check or preview exported files like KML or COLLADA, Google Earth Pro becomes a handy companion.

8. Google Earth Pro (Optional But Recommended)

Although Google Earth Pro isn’t strictly required to run 3DCityDB, it becomes incredibly useful once you start exporting your models. Many of the exercises in this tutorial series involve generating KML or COLLADA output, and Google Earth Pro remains one of the easiest tools to quickly inspect these files.

What makes it handy is that it renders textured CityGML features remarkably well — roofs, facades, and building surfaces appear exactly the way they should, which helps you verify whether the export settings were correct before moving on to more complex steps like tiling or web deployment.

If you’re following along with this tutorial series, it’s worth keeping Google Earth Pro installed. You’ll be using it to double-check exported buildings, walk around the model, and make sure everything aligns spatially.

📥 Download:

Google Earth

Download the installer, double-click it, and follow the on-screen instructions to complete the installation.

With all core components installed, your environment is fully ready. Now we can move on to the exciting part — setting up an empty database for CityGML models.

Conclusion: Your Foundation for 3DCityDB Is Now Ready

By now, you’ve walked through every essential component that powers a 3DCityDB environment — from installing Java and setting up PostgreSQL/PostGIS to configuring the Importer/Exporter tool, enabling plugins, preparing the course dataset, and launching the Web Map Client with Node.js.

If you’ve completed all the steps, congratulations: you now have a fully functional foundation for storing, managing, and visualizing 3D city models. Most beginners struggle not because 3DCityDB is difficult, but because the ecosystem around it can feel overwhelming at first. With this guide, you’ve built the entire pipeline piece by piece — and you understand why each tool exists and how they work together.

This is the moment when theory finally meets practice.

In the next part of this tutorial series, we’ll begin using these tools to create your first real database, import the Berlin CityGML sample, and explore it like an actual 3D city digital twin. You’ll learn:

  • how to set up your 3DCityDB schema
  • how to run your first CityGML import
  • how to query and inspect buildings
  • how to export your own 3D outputs

This is where the real fun begins — seeing your city model come alive in the database and inside a 3D viewer.

If you’re enjoying this hands-on series, make sure to follow for upcoming parts, where we’ll dive deeper into 3DCityDB, 3D Tiles, Cesium visualization, and digital twin workflows.

See you in Part 3 — let’s start building your first city! 🏙️🚀

30 Digital Twin Software Platforms to Know in 2025 — The Ultimate Breakdown

Below is a curated list of powerful tools and platforms used worldwide to create, manage, simulate, and visualize 3D city-scale digital twins.

Digital twins are no longer experimental side projects reserved for aerospace giants or advanced research labs. They have rapidly evolved into practical, scalable technologies for cities, utilities, transportation, construction, energy grids, and even environmental monitoring. But the backbone of every successful digital twin is the software ecosystem behind it.

From GIS engines and 3D city-modeling tools to IoT platforms, cloud services, simulation engines, and real-time visualization frameworks — each plays a distinct role in bringing a digital twin to life. And with hundreds of tools now available, the digital twin landscape can feel overwhelming, especially for newcomers trying to figure out where to begin.

This blog cuts through the noise.

Here, you’ll find a curated collection of 30 of the most widely used digital twin platforms in 2025 — tools trusted by governments, researchers, utilities, and smart-city innovators across the world. Whether you’re building a city-scale twin, a smart building platform, or a real-time urban dashboard, this list gives you a clear starting point for assembling your digital twin tech stack.

Let’s dive into the technologies shaping the next generation of intelligent, resilient, and data-driven environments.

1. ArcGIS CityEngine

A procedural 3D city-modeling tool by Esri, ideal for generating large-scale urban models from GIS footprints, terrain, and rule-based design.

Procedural City Generator | 3D City Maker | ArcGIS CityEngine

2. 3DCityDB

An open-source PostgreSQL/PostGIS database designed to store and manage semantic 3D city models (CityGML). A strong foundation for digital twin back-ends.

Redirecting

3. Cesium Platform

A high-performance 3D geospatial engine (WebGL/WebGPU) for streaming buildings, terrain, and real-time sensor data — widely used for interactive city twins.

Cesium: The Platform for 3D Geospatial

4. Azure Digital Twins

Microsoft’s cloud platform for modeling digital replicas of buildings, campuses, and cities, with IoT integration and real-time data relationships.

https://azure.microsoft.com/en-us/products/digital-twins/

5. iTwin Platform (Bentley Systems)

Infrastructure-focused digital twin solution supporting lifecycle management of bridges, roads, utilities, and city infrastructure.

How Digital Mirrors of the Real World Are Transforming the Way We Plan, Build, and Manage Urban Life

Cities today are no longer just physical spaces filled with buildings, roads, and utilities. They are dynamic ecosystems generating massive streams of data every second — from traffic signals and power grids to weather sensors and satellite imagery. As urban challenges grow more complex, so does the need for a smarter, more responsive way to understand, manage, and improve our cities.

This is where Digital Twins step in.

A digital twin is far more than a 3D model or a dashboard. It is a living mirror of the real world — a virtual city that sees what the physical city sees, learns from real-time data, simulates future scenarios, and helps planners, engineers, and citizens make better decisions. Whether it’s predicting floods, optimizing energy use, reducing traffic congestion, or improving infrastructure resilience, digital twins are rapidly becoming the backbone of modern urban innovation.

In this blog, we explore digital twins from the ground up — what they are, why they matter, how they evolved, and the technologies that make them possible. You’ll understand the complete workflow behind building a City-Scale Digital Twin, learn about the tools and platforms powering them (from ArcGIS CityEngine to Cesium, 3DCityDB, iTwin, and more), and dive into real urban use cases across planning, energy, disaster management, and mobility.

By the end of this guide, you’ll have a clear roadmap for starting your own digital twin project — from collecting datasets to integrating IoT feeds, building 3D models, running simulations, and deploying everything onto a unified interactive platform.

And this is just the beginning.

In the next blog, we will go hands-on with one of the most widely used open-source platforms for managing 3D city models — 3D City Database (3DCityDB). We will walk through the full beginner workflow, which includes installing the Importer/Exporter, setting up PostgreSQL and PostGIS, importing CityGML data, exporting 3D Tiles, integrating KML/COLLADA/glTF models, and visualizing them using the Cesium-based 3D Web Client. These practical exercises will help you actually build and visualize real city-scale digital twins step by step.

Welcome to the world of Digital Twins — where cities don’t just exist, they think, predict, and evolve.

Before we explore how digital twins are built and used today, it’s important to understand where the concept came from and how it evolved into the intelligent, real-time systems we see in modern cities.

A Digital Twin is a living digital model or a virtual copy of a real-world object, system, or process that is continuously updated with real-time data from sensors, devices, and other sources.

It acts like a mirror of the real world — showing how something is performing, how it’s likely to behave, and what can be improved — all inside a computer model.

It helps people monitor, analyze, and predict the performance of physical things — like cities, buildings, machines, or bridges — without being physically present.

History & Evolution of Digital Twins

How Digital Twins Evolved: From NASA to Smart Cities

Digital Twins may seem like a modern concept, but their roots go back more than 50 years. The idea started with engineering simulations and gradually evolved into today’s highly intelligent, real-time, AI-powered city-scale twins.

The Journey of Digital Twins: A Timeline

🔹 1960s–1970s — NASA’s Early Simulations
Engineers created physical duplicates and simulation models of spacecraft so they could troubleshoot and test changes without touching the real one.

🔹 2002 — First Formal Definition
Dr. Michael Grieves introduced the term “Digital Twin” in the context of Product Lifecycle Management (PLM).

🔹 2010–2015 — IoT Boom
Sensors became cheaper. Cloud computing became mainstream. Digital twins shifted from concept to practical use in manufacturing and aerospace.

🔹 2015–2020 — Rise of Smart Cities & Industry 4.0
Digital twins expanded into urban planning, utilities, mobility, energy, and environmental modeling.

🔹 2020–Present — AI-Driven Digital Twins
AI, real-time 3D visualization, and cloud streaming platforms (Cesium, Unity, Unreal, Omniverse) transformed digital twins into immersive, data-driven replicas of entire cities.

📖 Short Story: NASA’s Apollo Mission — The Birth of Digital Twins

During the Apollo 13 mission, NASA faced a near-catastrophic explosion onboard the spacecraft. To save the astronauts, engineers on Earth used an exact replica — same hardware, same configuration — to simulate every possible scenario and test solutions safely before sending instructions back to the crew.

This replica wasn’t called a “digital twin” at the time, but it was the first real use of the concept:

a model of the real system that mirrors its condition, allows simulation, and helps solve problems remotely.

Today’s digital twins are far more advanced — powered by real-time data streams, satellite imagery, AI, 3D models, and cloud computing — but the philosophy remains the same:

“Understand the real world better by recreating it in a virtual space.”

With this historical foundation in place, the next step is understanding the different forms digital twins can take — especially how each type functions within a city ecosystem.

2. Types of Digital Twins

Digital Twins come in multiple levels depending on how detailed and complex the representation is. In the context of cities, each type plays a unique role — ranging from modeling individual components (like a traffic light) to replicating the entire city ecosystem (like Singapore’s Virtual Singapore project).

🔹 1. Component Digital Twin

What it represents: A digital replica of a single physical part or component. Example: A smart streetlight with sensors measuring brightness, energy consumption, and pedestrian movement. Its digital twin monitors:

  • Lamp health
  • Energy usage patterns
  • Fault detection (e.g., flickering, outages)

This helps municipal teams optimize street lighting and reduce power consumption.

🔹 2. Asset Digital Twin

What it represents: A digital model of an individual asset composed of multiple components. Example: A traffic signal system at a busy intersection. The digital twin includes:

  • Controllers
  • Sensors
  • Pedestrian crossings
  • Real-time vehicle counts

The city can monitor peak traffic hours, predict congestion, and automatically adjust signal timings.

🔹 3. Process Digital Twin

What it represents: A twin that models an entire process or workflow rather than just an object. Example: A waste collection process for a city neighborhood. The digital twin simulates:

  • Garbage bin fill-level sensors
  • Truck routes
  • Fuel consumption
  • Time optimization for pickups

Result: Improved efficiency, reduced fuel costs, and cleaner streets.

🔹 4. System (or System-of-Systems) Digital Twin

What it represents: A combined digital twin of multiple interconnected assets and processes. This is the level where an entire city digital twin emerges. Example: A full urban mobility digital twin that integrates:

  • Metro and bus networks
  • Traffic systems
  • Pedestrian movement
  • Parking availability
  • Air quality sensors

This is the most comprehensive and intelligence-driven form of a digital twin.

Once we understand the different levels of twins, the natural question becomes: how do these diverse models stay consistent, compatible, and interoperable? This is where data standards become absolutely essential.

Importance of Data Standards

Why Data Standards Matter: CityGML, IFC, BIM, 3D Tiles

Data standards are the backbone of any successful digital twin. Without common formats, a city’s datasets — GIS layers, BIM models, traffic sensors, IoT feeds, LiDAR point clouds — sit in silos, unable to talk to each other. Standards ensure that 3D models, attributes, and sensor data can be shared, integrated, and visualized consistently across software platforms like Cesium, Autodesk, ArcGIS, and Bentley iTwin.

Here’s why standards are essential:

  • Interoperability: Ensures different systems (GIS, BIM, CAD, IoT) can communicate.
  • Accuracy: Preserves geometry, semantics, and relationships between city features.
  • Scalability: Allows large, multi-department city twins to evolve without breaking.
  • Longevity: Standard formats remain usable even when software changes.

Below are the major standards used in city digital twins:

CityGML

A standardized data model for representing 3D city objects — buildings, terrain, vegetation, water bodies, transportation networks.

  • Structured as Levels of Detail (LoD0–LoD4)
  • Highly semantic: includes building usage, height, roof type, etc.
  • Used by: 3DCityDB, Virtual Singapore, Berlin 3D Model, Rotterdam Twin

IFC (Industry Foundation Classes)

An open BIM standard used for storing detailed building and infrastructure models.

  • Contains walls, slabs, HVAC, MEP, materials, and construction schedules
  • Used for BIM-driven digital twins of buildings and facilities
  • Supported by: Autodesk Revit, Bentley, Graphisoft, Trimble

Example: A city integrates IFC models of new metro stations into its 3D city twin to analyze passenger flow and emergency evacuation scenarios.

BIM (Building Information Modeling)

BIM is not a file format — it’s a methodology. BIM models (IFC, RVT, etc.) represent building-level twins, describing:

  • Structural details
  • MEP systems
  • Asset metadata
  • Maintenance records

Example: In a smart campus, BIM twins of buildings connect to IoT sensors for real-time air quality and energy optimization.

3D Tiles (Cesium)

A modern, open standard for streaming massive 3D geospatial datasets on the web.

  • Streams large city models efficiently
  • Supports meshes, point clouds, and photogrammetry
  • Ideal for interactive city-scale visualization

Example: A city exports its entire 3D model to 3D Tiles to visualize traffic, IoT sensors, and construction updates in a browser-based digital twin dashboard.

Standards form the language of a digital twin — but building one requires far more than formats. To turn data into a living, urban-scale digital model, we need to understand its core technological components.

Critical Components of a City Digital Twin

Core Building Blocks of a City-Scale Digital Twin

A successful city digital twin is not built from a single technology — it is an ecosystem of integrated components working together to represent, monitor, simulate, and improve the real city.

A city-scale digital twin is built on a collection of deeply interconnected technologies that work together to create a living, breathing model of an urban environment. At its foundation is Geographic Information Systems (GIS), which provides the spatial context — maps, parcels, roads, utilities, terrain models — that form the backbone of a city twin. GIS ensures that every object, from a lamp post to a 50-storey building, is placed accurately in geographic space. Complementing GIS is Remote Sensing, which supplies high-resolution satellite imagery, LiDAR scans, drone photogrammetry, and thermal or hyperspectral imagery to build precise 3D models and detect real-world changes over time. These datasets allow the twin to stay updated with ground truth.

The next critical layer is IoT and sensor networks. Without real-time data, a digital twin is only a static 3D model. IoT feeds the twin with live streams of traffic counts, energy use, air quality levels, water pressure, weather conditions and more — turning the model into a dynamic “digital mirror” of the city. To make sense of this incoming data, cities depend on AI and Machine Learning, which perform demand forecasting, anomaly detection, behavioural predictions, and environmental simulations. In modern digital twins, AI is also used for automated change detection from satellite/drone imagery, and increasingly, Generative AI helps automate 3D modeling, scenario exploration, and conversational interactions with the twin.

Simulations form another indispensable component. Simulation engines such as traffic models, flood models, agent-based models, or energy simulations allow planners to test “what-if” scenarios before implementing solutions in the real world. These simulations are powered by Cloud Infrastructure, where massive datasets are stored, processed, and streamed. Cloud platforms enable scalability, high-performance computing, and complex analytics that city-scale digital twins require.

To bring everything to life visually, city twins rely on a 3D/Visualization Engine — often Cesium, Unreal Engine, Unity, Autodesk tools, or Esri’s CityEngine. These engines render 3D tiles, BIM objects, terrain, textures, lighting and real-time animations, making the twin intuitive and immersive. Today, cities are also starting to integrate AR and VR, allowing planners to walk inside a digital building, inspect underground utilities, or visualize future city plans in mixed reality environments.

Finally, several emerging technologies are enhancing trust, security and efficiency. Blockchain is being explored to guarantee data integrity, audit sensor inputs, or track infrastructure lifecycle events. Edge Computing supports faster processing by handling sensor data directly at the source — reducing latency for applications like traffic signal optimisation or emergency response. Together, these technologies form the core building blocks of a modern city digital twin, transforming raw data into an intelligent, interactive, and continually evolving model of urban life.

These technologies work together, but they need a clear structural blueprint. To see how everything connects behind the scenes, we now look at the architecture that powers a digital twin.

Architecture of a Digital Twin

A digital twin may look like a single unified model from the outside, but behind the scenes, it is built on a layered, interconnected architecture that brings together data, computation, and visualization into one living system. At its core, a digital twin integrates three worlds: the physical environment, the digital representation, and the data exchange layer that keeps them synchronized.

The first layer is the physical environment, the real-world system being mirrored. In the case of a city digital twin, this includes buildings, roads, utilities, mobility networks, landscapes, sensors, and anything that generates data. This physical layer constantly produces raw inputs — from IoT sensors, satellites, drones, LiDAR scanners, CCTV feeds, weather stations, traffic counters, smart meters, or even citizen-generated data.

The second layer is the data ingestion and integration layer, which captures this real-world information and funnels it into the digital twin. This is where data pipelines, ETL workflows, and streaming protocols operate. Technologies such as MQTT, REST APIs, cloud IoT hubs, geospatial servers, and remote sensing workflows transform all incoming information into structured datasets. At this stage, accepted standards like CityGML, IFC, BIM, GeoJSON, 3D Tiles, LandUse codes, and metadata specifications are crucial — they ensure that diverse datasets can speak the same language and fit into a unified model.

Once the data is ingested, the third layer — data management and storage — organizes it into an accessible, scalable system. This layer typically includes geospatial databases (PostGIS, 3DCityDB), BIM repositories, time-series databases for sensor feeds, cloud object storage for large imagery or point clouds, and metadata registries. This is the “memory” of the twin, holding everything from historical data and 3D models to IoT time-series streams and simulation inputs.

Above this sits the modeling and analytics layer, where intelligence happens. Here, simulation engines, AI/ML models, physics-based solvers, and geospatial analytics process the data to make predictions, generate alerts, and test scenarios. Whether it’s predicting flooding in a low-lying neighborhood, estimating building energy usage, simulating traffic routing, or detecting structural stress in a bridge, this analytical layer gives the digital twin its predictive and prescriptive capabilities. It also connects with domain-specific engines such as energy simulators, hydrologic models, finite element analysis tools, or agent-based mobility models.

The next layer is the 3D representation and visualization engine, where all information becomes interactive. Tools such as Cesium, Unreal Engine, Unity, CityEngine, or custom WebGL/WebGPU engines render the city in 3D. This is where maps, buildings, vegetation, infrastructure networks, and live sensor feeds are unified into a visually intuitive experience. For users, this is the face of the digital twin — an interactive environment where they can explore, query, and understand the system in real time.

Finally, the top layer is the user interaction and application layer, consisting of dashboards, analytics interfaces, APIs, mobile apps, decision-support tools, and command-center views. This layer shapes how planners, engineers, citizens, policymakers, and emergency responders interact with the digital twin. Whether it’s a real-time air quality map, a construction monitoring dashboard, or a predictive flood simulation panel, this application layer connects insights to action.

Together, these layers form the architectural backbone of a digital twin — continuously sensing, thinking, and visualizing. It is this architecture that transforms raw, chaotic data from the physical world into a dynamic, intelligent system capable of guiding decisions, optimizing operations, and predicting the future of a city.

Understanding the architecture makes it easier to appreciate what digital twins can actually do. With the foundations in place, we can now explore the real-world benefits they bring to cities and industries.

🔹 Benefits of Digital Twins

1. Real-Time Monitoring

A digital twin allows continuous, real-time monitoring of physical assets, systems, or environments. Sensors and IoT devices collect live data — such as temperature, energy use, or air quality — and feed it into the digital model. This helps city planners, engineers, or operators observe what’s happening at any given moment. Example: In a smart city, digital twins track traffic flow and air pollution levels in real time, allowing authorities to respond quickly to congestion or poor air quality.

2. Predictive Maintenance

By analyzing patterns in live and historical data, digital twins can predict when equipment or infrastructure might fail. This means maintenance can be done before problems occur, reducing costly downtime and repairs. Example: In a smart building, sensors on HVAC systems send performance data to a digital twin that predicts when a unit will need servicing, preventing system breakdowns.

3. Scenario Simulation

Digital twins make it possible to simulate “what-if” scenarios without experimenting in the real world. Planners and engineers can test how a change — like new construction, traffic rerouting, or extreme weather — would affect the system. Example: Urban planners can use a city’s digital twin to simulate heavy rainfall and identify flood-prone areas before a storm occurs.

4. Improved Decision-Making

Because digital twins combine real-world data with predictive models, they provide decision-makers with deep insights for smarter planning and resource allocation. Decisions become data-driven rather than assumption-based. Example: Utility managers can use a water network’s digital twin to identify pressure issues, plan pipe replacements, and optimize water distribution efficiency.

5. Cost and Time Efficiency

A digital twin helps reduce costs and save time by detecting inefficiencies early and minimizing trial-and-error in design or operations. Since simulations replace physical testing, resources are conserved.
Example: Construction teams use digital twins of buildings to detect design flaws virtually before actual construction begins, avoiding expensive rework later.

6. Enhanced Design and Innovation

Engineers and designers use digital twins to test and refine designs continuously using real-world feedback. As data accumulates, models evolve, leading to innovation and performance improvement over time.
Example: Automotive companies like Tesla use digital twins to analyze how cars perform in real-world driving and improve future vehicle models.

7. Collaboration and Visualization

Digital twins provide interactive 3D visualization of complex systems, helping teams from different departments understand and collaborate easily. They serve as a single source of truth where everyone can see the same data and models. Example: City planners, utility managers, and architects can all view the same 3D digital twin of a city, enabling coordinated decisions about roadworks, zoning, and public utilities.

8. Sustainability and Energy Optimization

By continuously tracking energy use and environmental conditions, digital twins help optimize resource consumption and promote sustainability. They identify wasteful patterns and suggest more efficient alternatives. Example: In smart campuses, building twins automatically adjust lighting and air conditioning based on occupancy, saving energy and reducing carbon emissions.

9. Risk Reduction and Disaster Preparedness

Digital twins support risk analysis and emergency planning by simulating natural disasters, accidents, or system failures. They help authorities design safer, more resilient systems.
Example: Flood-prone cities like Singapore and Rotterdam use digital twins to simulate water flow and plan better drainage and evacuation strategies.

10. Lifecycle Management

Digital twins represent assets throughout their entire lifecycle — from design and construction to operation, maintenance, and eventual decommissioning. This continuous data connection ensures better asset health and long-term performance.
Example: Infrastructure managers maintain a digital twin of bridges or tunnels to track structural changes, enabling safe operation and efficient maintenance over decades.

🏙️ Workflow of Creating a City Digital Twin

Knowing what digital twins can achieve, the next question is: how do we actually build one? Let’s walk through the complete end-to-end workflow of creating a city-scale digital twin.

Building a city-scale digital twin is not a single action but a multi-layered process that brings together data engineering, 3D modelling, IoT integration, and simulation technologies. The workflow typically begins with defining the purpose of the twin — whether the goal is urban planning, disaster resilience, energy optimisation, traffic management, or simply centralised monitoring. Without a clear objective, the twin easily becomes an expensive 3D model with no real intelligence. So the first step is always framing the vision: What will the digital twin solve? Who will use it? What data is required?

Once the goals are defined, cities move into the data-collection phase. This involves gathering geospatial information such as cadastral maps, land-use layers, road networks, utility lines, and administrative boundaries. Remote sensing data — satellite imagery, aerial photography, and LiDAR scans — help reconstruct the physical form of the city. BIM models contribute interior details for complex buildings, while IoT sensors provide real-time updates on traffic, air quality, water distribution, energy consumption, and environmental conditions. At this point, the city is essentially collecting its “digital DNA.”

The next step involves integrating and harmonising these datasets. Cities rarely store information in one place, which means incoming data arrives in multiple formats — CityGML, IFC, Shapefiles, GeoJSON, CSV, 3D Tiles, and even scanned PDFs. This stage demands strong GIS workflows, data cleaning, projection alignment, and establishing a unified spatial reference system. The goal is to make everything interoperable so that the digital twin becomes a living ecosystem rather than a fragmented collection of files.

Once the data foundation is set, the 3D city model begins to take shape. Tools like CityEngine, ArcGIS Urban, FME, Blender, or 3D Tiles pipelines are used to reconstruct buildings, terrain, vegetation, utility networks, and public spaces. Some cities adopt Level of Detail (LOD) modelling, where simple extruded footprints represent large areas, while high-detail photogrammetry or BIM enrich priority locations. At this stage, the digital twin becomes visually explorable — forming a spatial canvas on which intelligence will be layered.

Real-time integration is what transforms a 3D model into an actual digital twin. IoT devices, traffic sensors, environmental monitors, energy meters, CCTV feeds, and weather stations constantly push new information into the system. Cloud platforms, APIs, MQTT streams, and data brokers ensure that the virtual city remains synchronised with the physical one. Every piece of data, from the water level in a canal to the movement of a bus, becomes a living input feeding the twin.

After integrating live data, cities add intelligence through analytics, AI models, and simulations. This is where digital twins become powerful decision-making tools. Machine learning predicts traffic congestion, flooding, infrastructure stress, or energy consumption. Simulation engines help run what-if experiments — How will a new flyover affect congestion? What happens if rainfall increases by 20%? Where should emergency responders be positioned during a major event? At this stage, the digital twin is no longer just a model — it becomes a predictive and prescriptive system.

The final layer involves building visualisation interfaces and interactive dashboards. These may take the form of 3D web platforms, immersive AR/VR environments, or city command-and-control dashboards. Planners, policymakers, researchers, and citizens can view the city from multiple perspectives, explore data layers, run scenarios, and make informed decisions. Accessibility and user experience become just as important as technical accuracy.

A city digital twin is never “finished.” It must evolve continuously — updated with new satellite imagery, revised zoning maps, IoT data, construction progress, policy changes, and environmental observations. Governance frameworks ensure data quality, security, and privacy as the system scales. Over time, the twin becomes a long-term digital infrastructure asset, supporting everything from climate resilience to mobility planning and sustainable development.

⭐ 30 Software Platforms for Building 3D City Digital Twins

Below is a curated list of powerful tools and platforms used worldwide to create, manage, simulate, and visualize 3D city-scale digital twins.

1. ArcGIS CityEngine

A procedural 3D city-modeling tool by Esri, ideal for generating large-scale urban models from GIS footprints, terrain, and rule-based design.

Procedural City Generator | 3D City Maker | ArcGIS CityEngine

2. 3DCityDB

An open-source PostgreSQL/PostGIS database designed to store and manage semantic 3D city models (CityGML). A strong foundation for digital twin back-ends.

Redirecting

3. Cesium Platform

A high-performance 3D geospatial engine (WebGL/WebGPU) for streaming buildings, terrain, and real-time sensor data — widely used for interactive city twins.

Cesium: The Platform for 3D Geospatial

4. Azure Digital Twins

Microsoft’s cloud platform for modeling digital replicas of buildings, campuses, and cities, with IoT integration and real-time data relationships.

https://azure.microsoft.com/en-us/products/digital-twins/

5. iTwin Platform (Bentley Systems)

Infrastructure-focused digital twin solution supporting lifecycle management of bridges, roads, utilities, and city infrastructure.

Digital Twins | Infrastructure Digital Twin Software

6. TwinCity3D

An urban digital twin tool for creating, managing, and sharing 3D city dashboards, planning scenarios, and decision-making workflows.

Revolutionizing Urban Digital Twins with Open Source Technology

7. VU.CITY

A detailed, photorealistic 3D digital twin of major cities used for planning, visualization, and stakeholder engagement.

VU.CITY | Visualise, Model and Understand Urban Change in 3D

8. Autodesk Tandem
